newsitem.title: FRANCE: France trumpets jobless dip, opposition doubts data.
newsitem.headline: France trumpets jobless dip, opposition doubts data.

text.p: France's centre-right government trumpeted a dip in unemployment on Wednesday ahead of a snap parliamentary election, but opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said the statistics were rigged.

On the far right, National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said he had decided against running in the May 25-June 1 National Assembly vote. He denied it was because opinion polls show he is unlikely to win one of the 577 seats.

The last unemployment figures to be released before the election showed a dip of 4,800 people in the giant jobless total to 3,087,500 in March, according to national criteria. It was the second slight fall in a row.
But the jobless rate calculated by International Labour Organisation (ILO) rules remained at a record 12.8 percent of the workforce and Jospin said the figures understated the numbers of unemployed.

"One doesn't have the right, when one claims to lead France...to rig the figures," he said in Aulnay-sous-Bois near Paris. He said government statistics "conjured away" 300,000 unemployed people who were previously counted.
Opinion polls show joblessness is voters' number one concern.

Allies of conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe, whose popularity has sunk as unemployment has risen from 11.7 percent when he took office in 1995, said the March figures showed the rise in unemployment had stopped.
"One can consider that since the last quarter of 1996, the rise in unemployment has been stopped," Labour Minister Jacques Barrot said.
Le Pen, who wants to send home three million immigrants, ended days of speculation by announcing he would not run.

He accused President Jacques Chirac of wanting to stifle political sleaze scandals by calling the snap election almost 10 months early and said Chirac should resign if his centre-right allies failed to win at least half the vote.

"I will not present myself for legislative elections, thinking that I will have better things to do in preparing for possible presidential elections," Le Pen said. Chirac has ruled out resigning before the end of his seven-year term in 2002.

Le Pen, who won 15 percent of the vote in 1995 presidential elections, denied he was scared that his leadership would be weakened if he ran and failed to win, especially if other National Front politicians squeezed in.
The party has no seats in parliament but has set itself a target of winning 20. Opinion polls show it has a chance of winning a handful at best.

On the left, the opposition Socialists and tiny Greens party, battling polls indicating the government is likely to retain power, agreed on joint candidates in 106 constituencies as part of a left-wing unity drive.

"For the first time in their history, the Greens will be able to enter the National Assembly," Greens leader Dominique Voynet predicted at a joint news conference with Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin.
The joint candidacies will give the Socialists a head start in the horse trading which takes place before the second round run-off votes in seats where no one wins a first round majority.
The Communist Party and the tiny Citizens' Movement, which has four seats in parliament, also agreed on joint candidacies in 44 constituencies -- 30 Communists and 14 from the MDC.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe got bad news from an opinion poll showing his popularity had dipped to match last year's all-time low. The CSA survey showed he won a favourable rating from just 28 percent, down two points from March, with 65 percent against.
Forty-one percent expressed support for Chirac, up from 36 percent, with 55 percent against.
